Anthropic’s network and Congress

450 of 533

More than four in five members of Congress have a documented tie to Anthropic’s network: the company, the funders behind it, the groups they fund, and their PACs and lobbyists. A tie is a public record; for 118 of the 450 it records only what third parties did. This is that record, and how fast it was made.

Each dot is one of the 533 members serving on Nov. 26, 2026. A tie is a public record that links the member and the network: a contribution, a lobbying report on the member’s bill, a fellow in the office, a statement.

Third parties are lobbyists at the network’s lobbying firms, who gave their own money, and super PACs that received network money and made their own expenditures. A tie can cut either way: a statement may be criticism, and a super PAC may have spent against the member. It is not an allegation, and a contribution is not a vote.

Start with the company: its employees’ own gifts, and its PAC’s.

What counts as a tie: the eleven kinds of record

A tie is one or more public records that link a member now serving and the network. Each count is the members with at least one record of that kind.

I · The arrival

At the end of 2024, 10 members now serving had received money from Anthropic’s employees or its PAC. By Sept. 30, 2026: 196.

The employees gave their own money: $5.6M, 92% of it dated 2026. The company’s PAC made its first gift on record to a member now serving on June 29, 2026; by Sept. 30 it had given $200K to 81 members, 18 of whom had no gift from an employee.

Source: FEC contribution records in this project’s tables: contributions to the campaign, leadership PAC or single-member joint fundraising committee of a serving member, through Sept. 30, 2026; ANTHROPAC is Anthropic PBC’s political action committee.

A person’s contribution is their own money, not their employer’s. Employer is as the giver reported it to the FEC. Both counts are of the members serving on Nov. 26, 2026; the record stops at Sept. 30, 2026.

How many people wrote those checks?

Every gift on record to a member now serving: 1,027 from Anthropic’s employees, 87 from its PAC

Through Sept. 30, 2026. The scale is logarithmic: each line is ten times the one below. Dots are translucent, so a bright patch is many gifts of one size on nearby dates.

I · The arrival

Ten givers account for 58% of the employees’ dollars.

The filings list 89 distinct names with Anthropic as employer; together they gave $5.6M. Half of them gave $20,500 or less. The two largest gave $553K and $545K, spread across 70 and 65 members.

Each circle is one name as filed, a first name and a surname; its area is what that name gave to members now serving. The smallest circles are drawn a little larger than scale, so that each can be seen.

Givers are private individuals and are not named here. The count is of first names and surnames as filed: two people who share both would count as one.

Where did it land?

I · The arrival

Democrats received 55% of the dollars. But six of the ten largest recipients are Republicans.

Employees’ gifts and the PAC’s together went to 111 Democrats and 84 Republicans. Jon Ossoff, a Democrat, received the most: $218K.

Source: FEC contribution records; all years on record, through Sept. 30, 2026.

Totals are by member: campaign, leadership PAC and single-member joint fundraising committees together. A total is what the committees received, not what a member asked for. The ranking does not hang on the cut-off: Republicans are more than half of the five largest recipients, and of every longer list up to fourteen.

$5.8M in all. The large money moved another way.

II · The bigger money

Anthropic announced $40.0M for Public First Action. A super PAC that group funds reported $15.0M of independent spending for one House candidate.

Two separate records, not one stream. No dollar can be followed from one to the other.

Source: Anthropic’s announcements; FEC contribution and outside-spending reports of the Public First committees. Not drawn: $1.0M Public First Action passed to a third committee, and one $105K ad naming a member without saying for or against.

No filing in this record lists Public First Action’s donors; the two gifts are as Anthropic announced them. The super PACs reported the spending as independent expenditures. A contribution does not direct spending.

The company’s funders gave more, and for longer.

The 15 candidates the two super PACs spent for or against

Independent spending reported to the FEC in 2026, by the super PAC that spent and the race it named. Four of the 15 now serve in Congress; the spending that named them was all for them.

II · The bigger money

The network gave 26 committees $200M; they spent $541M, from all their donors, for or against members, $420M of it against Republicans.

Half of the $200M is Dustin Moskovitz’s $100M to FF PAC (he gave outside groups $130M in 2016–2024). FF PAC spent $11.2M of the $541M; the top spender took in $5.3M.

Two separate records on one scale; no dollar is traced from a gift to an expenditure.

Source: FEC outside-spending reports naming a member now serving; the same 26 committees’ receipts on record from the network (transfers among the Public First committees counted once). Of the $200M, $40.0M is as Anthropic announced it. Not in the $200M: $420K the two Public First super PACs report from other donors, $205K of it in three gifts from two people who list Anthropic as their employer.

A contribution does not direct spending; independent spending is not coordination; a member opposed received nothing.

One kind of money reaches more members than any of this, and the network did not give it.

The 26 committees, who gave, and which members the spending named

II · The bigger money

No tie reaches more members than lobbyists’ own gifts: 323 received $1.4M from lobbyists at firms with a network client.

For 299 of them a giver is named on that client’s own filings; for the other 24, only the givers’ firms are registered for it. It is third parties’ money: for 83 of the 323, third-party records are all there is on file.

Counted: a gift whose giver was a registered lobbyist at a firm that had a network client in that period. Each lit seat received at least one.

Source: lobbyists’ semi-annual contribution reports to Congress, Feb. 19, 2021 to June 30, 2026; FEC records tie each receiving committee to one member.

The money is the lobbyist’s own, not the client’s, and the record does not say why a gift was made. Named lobbyists only: $1.2M in 994 gifts.

Lobbyists are paid to ask. Here is what Anthropic spent.

Lobbyists’ own gifts to members now serving, by election cycle

74 lobbyists at 23 firms made the 1,152 gifts: 153 Democrats, 169 Republicans and one independent received at least one. The total has grown in each cycle; for 2026, the reports read so far stop at June 30.

III · The lobbying

Anthropic’s reported lobbying spending is up twentyfold since 2023: $280K that year, $5.6M in the first nine months of 2026.

The 2023 sum is what outside firms reported being paid to lobby for Anthropic; the 2026 sum is the lobbying expenses on the company’s own reports, January to September.

Source: quarterly lobbying reports (form LD-2) through Sept. 30, 2026, for Anthropic and the nine other highest-spending network clients in the years drawn; for the shares, the 2019–2025 reports this project classified as naming AI or an AI bill by title, after its documented exclusions.

Amounts are as filed, rounded. A quarter with the company’s own report leaves out its outside firms’ reports. A report’s amount covers every issue on it, so the two shares of the field are of report totals, not of AI lobbying; 2025 is the last full year compared.

Small beside the field. But which bills did its reports name?

What was reported in 2025 on lobbying reports that name AI, at about $1M a square

1,211 squares after rounding. The six gold ones are all the network’s groups together in 2025: $5.6M. That is not the $5.6M on the line chart, which is Anthropic alone in January to September 2026. Each report’s amount covers every issue on it, so these are upper bounds on AI lobbying. Over 2024–25, Anthropic ($3.9M) reported less than OpenAI ($4.8M) and far less than Meta ($50.7M).

III · The lobbying

The three bills most named in lobbying reports filed for Anthropic are about chips. All six sponsors received gifts from Anthropic’s employees or its PAC.

The gifts are a separate record, the FEC’s: $328,500 in all. None of the 68 reports states a position on a bill.

Source: the 68 quarterly lobbying reports filed for Anthropic, 2023 to Sept. 30, 2026 (each bill described from its official title); FEC contribution records.

A report that names a bill says the client lobbied on it, not which way and not whether a sponsor’s office was contacted. The gifts are individuals’ own or the PAC’s. No filing in this record ties a gift to a bill.

How often did a sponsor also receive a gift?

The four bills most named in lobbying reports filed for Anthropic

Of the 68 reports filed for Anthropic, 18 name a bill. Each bill is shown with words excerpted from its official title as introduced (Government Publishing Office bill status files), its House and Senate numbers and its sponsors now serving; each dot is one quarterly report that names it. Annual defence and spending bills are not ranked (none is named as often as these three); House and Senate versions count as one bill where a report pairs them.

III · The lobbying

Lobbying reports filed for Anthropic name bills by 23 members. 19 of them received gifts from Anthropic’s employees or its PAC.

Among the 91 sponsors of AI bills with no bill of theirs named in a network report, it was 47; in all of Congress, 196 of 533. By chamber: 12 of the 13 senators against 60 of all 100, and 7 of the 10 House members against 136 of all 433.

A report that names a bill says the client lobbied on it: not which way, and not whether the sponsor’s office was contacted.

Source: quarterly lobbying reports filed for Anthropic, matched to verified sponsors (annual defence and spending bills not counted); AI bills from this project’s companion study; FEC contribution records through Sept. 30, 2026.

No money is attributed to the lobbying; each gift is an individual’s own or the PAC’s. Which came first, a gift or a report, says nothing about why either was made. “Filed for Anthropic” means the company’s own report or one by a firm it hired.

The gifts and the lobbying are recent. The grants are older.

The 38 members whose bills the network’s lobbying reports name

Reports filed for Anthropic name bills by 23 of them; reports filed for the network’s other groups name bills by 15 more. With both counted, 27 of the 38 received a gift from Anthropic’s employees or its PAC. Each dot is one quarterly report naming a bill the member sponsored; the bar and the sum are those gifts, all years on record.

IV · The decade before

By the end of 2024, seven of the network’s funders had already awarded $528M in grants, and Congress was hearing from their grantees.

By then, ten of the members now serving had received money from Anthropic’s employees or its PAC. The grants paid for work on AI, technology, biosecurity and catastrophic risk; none of the grants shown names a member of Congress as its recipient.

Source: IRS Form 990 grant schedules and the funders’ own published grant lists; witness lists from congress.gov, House committee pages and Senate hearing transcripts.

A grant to an organisation is not money to a member, and an award is not a payment on its date. Two of the ten largest grantees have a witness in this record.

Witnesses visit. Who works inside?

The 49 appearances, the grants by year and the 12 largest grantees

An appearance counts when the witness list names the witness in a grantee’s role, from the date the network first funded that line of the organisation’s work: 17 earlier appearances are left out, and for RAND, CNAS and Carnegie testimony counts where it is on work the network funds. Each appearance is at a committee’s invitation; testifying is not lobbying, and nothing in this record ties a grant to an appearance or to a person. Two of the ten largest grantees have a witness in this record, CSET and RAND. Jason Matheny is counted three times as RAND’s president; two more hearings where he spoke in that role are on record outside the count. Institute for Progress’s grants are general support, counted under another cause.

IV · The decade before

Horizon, a network grantee, has funded 25 fellows in Congress since 2022: in offices of both parties, on committees and commissions.

Horizon says the host manages a fellow’s work. Separately, eight of the nine senators who hosted a fellow have received money from Anthropic’s employees or its PAC, as have 60 of all 100 senators.

Each dot is one placement since 2022, as the programme’s roster lists it.

Source: Horizon Institute placement pages and alumni lists, and its “Host a Fellow” and “About” pages as saved in 2026; IRS Form 990 grant schedules; FEC contribution records through Sept. 30, 2026.

No gift is tied to a placement. A gift is its giver’s money: an employee’s own, or the PAC’s. Horizon’s own page says no single funder provides a majority of its money.

People cross the other way, too.

Where the 29 placements were: 20 offices, committees and commissions

As the programme’s roster lists them, with the year each placement began (one has no year on the roster, and one host has since left Congress). Fellows are counted, not named.

IV · The decade before

64 people went from Congress to positions with the network or its lobbying firms; most had been staff.

At least eight had been members. Nine of the positions are advisory, board or trustee seats, and for two no title is printed. The 26 who came the other way are Horizon fellows: the 25 of the last slide and one at the Government Accountability Office, a legislative‑branch agency.

Each dot is one person. The gold line is the door between Congress and the network.

Source: House and Senate payroll reports, fellowship pages, lobbyists’ disclosed former posts and organisations’ staff pages.

Taking a job or a seat is not evidence about the work done in it. Each person counts once per direction.

Grants, hearings, fellows, jobs, money. Add it up.

V · The sum

239 of the 450 have only one or two kinds of record. For 118 of them, every record is of what third parties did.

Third parties are lobbyists at the network’s lobbying firms, who gave their own money, and super PACs that received network money and made their own expenditures. Thom Tillis has one kind of record: $42.1M that super PACs reported spending in opposition.

Each dot is one of the 533 members, in the column for the number of kinds of record on file. A kind counts once, however many records or dollars it holds.

Source: the record’s member table; 11 kinds of record, two of them records of what third parties did (lobbyists’ own gifts, super PAC spending).

The record shows the network money the super PACs received and the super PACs’ spending separately; it does not trace one to the other. Outside spending is not coordination with the candidate, and a lobbyist’s gift is the lobbyist’s own money.

So what does the whole record show?

The 17 members with six or more kinds of record

A kind counts once, however many records or dollars it holds, and it can cut either way: a statement may be criticism, and a super PAC may have spent against the member. A faint dot means no counted record was found, not that none exists.

V · The sum

A record of ties, not a record of influence.

The opening slide’s 533 seats again, by party. A ring is a member with only records of what third parties did.

Members serving on Nov. 26, 2026; records through Sept. 30, 2026.

How this was counted: the eleven kinds of record, by party, and the rows collected

Records through Sept. 30, 2026; independent audits of the latest update were still open on Nov. 26, 2026. The 29 source figures, the tables and the method are in the repository.
